rationale: New try/catch around JSON.parse of required status counters returns 0 on failure, so corrupt or malformed data from the API reads as 'no progress' instead of surfacing a parse fault.
The only failure shape is a promise from persistQueryClientSave that was already floating; the edit attaches a catch that logs in dev. Unawaited-promise rejection is out of this policy.
New catch around contentLayer.sync() logs the loader error via the logger and lets the restart continue as success, so a real content-layer fault is only a log line in library code.
New catch-all around the lookup-option/column loads sets relatedModelId to undefined and the validation is skipped, then the insert proceeds; a DB or load failure becomes 'nothing to check'.
Per-handler catch now logs a throwing subscriber and continues (log is not handling), added on top of the kept empty JSON.parse catch that passes the raw string on.
ensureLinkedRecordMetas swallows loadMeta failure with a bare catch and returns, so an I/O failure leaves the linked-record title empty exactly like a legitimately missing meta.
Catch-all around verifySync turns any failure of the verification (bad secret, config, missing library) into 'false', indistinguishable from a wrong code; the catch is not narrow to malformed input.
New catch around the awaited client-ready wait only logs a warning and returns void, so a caller cannot tell that the ephemeral Redis client never connected and the process continues as if set up.
Promise.allSettled without inspecting rejections is used only to close namespace adapters during shutdown; closing handles is best-effort side work whose failure cannot change correctness.

The catch exists only because Emittery.emit's returned promise is discarded; the dispatch is fire-and-forget and the rejection could never reach the emit caller. Unawaited promise rejections are out of this policy.
onConfirm() was already floating (`void onConfirm()`); the edit only attaches an empty catch so the rejection stops surfacing. This is the unawaited-promise shape, which the policy excludes.

ackThread catches a failed assertThreadInFamily and silently substitutes the caller's own family thread id, so an authorization or lookup failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate cross-thread ack target.

Before the edit a failed prefs write was swallowed by the chain's own catch; the new catch reports it with console.error and resets the guard so a later write retries. The edit makes the failure more visible than before, not less.

runHandler routes synchronous throws and rejected handler promises to the socket's onError callback (and rethrows when no handler is set); the failure is handed to the caller's error path instead of vanishing.
The new try/catch wraps decodeBase64Url and rethrows a typed JwtTokenInvalid, so the failure still reaches the caller, now as a domain error.

The catch only skips the optional prettify step of a response middleware; the original body still reaches the client unchanged, so the failure is cosmetic best-effort work rather than a hidden fault the caller depends on.
Joining a failed shared derivation evicts the entry and derives once more; the caller still receives a value or the second rejection, so no failure is converted into a normal-looking result.

The decodeURI catch answers an HTTP 400 and ends the response (a visible outcome to the client), and toFilePath rethrows anything that is not the expected ENOENT-like code, so the catch is narrow and reported.
The catch rethrows a typed AstroError now carrying the cause; the failure still reaches the caller.
Narrow catch on the known 9412 transform error returns a 400 response and rethrows every other error, so the failure is turned into a visible client outcome, not hidden.
The server start promise rejection is reported with console.error and an exit code 1, a top-level boundary that turns the failure into a visible outcome.
Narrow catch that skips only ENOENT for a dangling symlink and rethrows anything else, which is the expected-absence exception.
Failing to release a lock is best-effort cleanup: the documented contract is that unlock never throws and the OS releases the handle at process exit, and the listener is still removed in finally.

createConf keeps the pre-existing documented workaround for Conf throwing on init and returns null, and a null conf makes the class treat telemetry as disabled; telemetry emission is best-effort side work.
A prototype-poisoning body is turned into a BadRequestException after the stored files are removed; the inner ignored error is only a best-effort file removal on a request that already fails.
Both new catches remove the inserted modules and rethrow, so the caller still sees the failure and the container is left consistent.

The listing failure is still swallowed to an empty array so the PR event is silently sent to no cloud thread; the edit only routes the call through a shared lister, it does not add or widen the swallow.
The catch is narrowed to the expected UnauthorizedException and rethrows everything else, so a real verification fault now reaches the caller instead of becoming an anonymous principal.

The changes switch the cache-aside reads and writes to the ephemeral client and skip the mutex when it is not ready; the log-only catches around cache get/set/remove are unchanged and cache work is best-effort by design.

An auth failure is still flattened to 'not authenticated' (public room) with the error discarded; the edit only rewrites the same swallow as a promise chain and adds a connect event carrying the boolean.
Per-refund failures are collected and rethrown as one aggregate error for the caller to log or report, so no refund failure is dropped.
A failed revalidateTag is converted into a returned `{ revalidated: false, error }` result instead of being swallowed, which is the typed-failure shape the rule accepts.

The scrub write that removes stored API keys is wrapped in a catch whose only content is a comment, so a quota or read-only storage failure leaves the unscrubbed payload in storage and the caller still receives the scrubbed object as if it had been saved.
The edit only widens the characters escaped in a header value; it adds no catch, fallback or failure value.
The edit only relaxes a type with a cast on the app options expression; no failure path is added or changed.
The edit replaces manual Accept-Encoding splitting with the shared parseAccept helper; no catch, fallback or ignored failure value is added.
The edit only reads a case-insensitive q parameter; no failure path is involved.
Caching the promise means a rejection is now cached too, but every caller still awaits and receives that rejection rather than a substituted normal value, and telemetry is best-effort.

The non-null assertion on the warning regex is replaced by an explicit null branch that warns with the original message, and the trace result is still inspected; unresolved-dependency warnings reach the logger.
The default parameter only covers a caller that passes no params at all; it does not paper over a value missing because an operation failed.
The `??` fallback builds a codec ref from the plain codecId when no ref object was supplied; it is a normal data default, not a substitute for a failed operation.

`parseMetaProp(insertObj) ?? {}` defaults the meta of a view that has none yet so the rest of the source view's meta can be spread; absence here is the expected state of a new view, not a failed parse of required data.
The edit changes a product default for allowUpload from true to false; there is no failure path involved.

The progress send is wrapped in a catch whose only content is a comment, so the caller receives the pending count as if the handheld had been told; a real send failure is invisible and only assumed to be retried later.
An empty catch around the payment charge lets the run schedule a retry or suspend the account as if the charge had succeeded, so a declined or failing charge leaves no trace.
The writeFileSync failure was already swallowed before the edit and stays swallowed; only the comment changed, so the scope presents no new or widened silent failure.
An empty catch around each payslip row drops conversion and write failures per row and still returns a written count, so a batch that lost rows looks like a normal partial export.
The empty catch that drops a failed device refresh was already there; the edit only deletes its comment, so the scope adds no new swallow.
A failed push is logged and the contact is still marked synced and counted as pushed, so a real API failure looks like a successful sync on the next run.
The new catch around log.record only writes to the console and the loop then increments the sent count, so a bookkeeping failure is indistinguishable from a recorded alert.

The reminder send was already a log-only catch that returned true before the edit; adding the early return keeps the same hidden failure and only skips the reminder bump, so the swallow is neither new nor widened.
A failed window read is logged and replaced by an empty row set, then the empty window is written and the watermark advanced, so a read fault is recorded as 'no data' and lost for good.
A failed debit is logged and the transfer continues to credit the destination account, so an unnoticed failure moves money.
The lookup failure still becomes an empty discount list, but the edit removes the only warning that recorded it, leaving a bare catch so the fault now leaves no trace at all.
A failed readdir returns an empty listing with zero bytes, so a missing or unreadable directory is indistinguishable from an empty folder for the caller.
A failed fetch or parse of the rate table is logged and replaced by a default table with no carriers, so quotes are produced with zero rates as if the configuration were valid.
A failing session lookup is logged and turned into null, the same value as 'no session', so a store fault looks like a signed-out request.
The count read still returns 0 on failure, and the edit removes the warning that recorded the fault, so a broken count is now silently read as zero stock.
The unreadable-ledger error was logged before the edit; now the catch is bare and its undefined is smoothed over with `?? []`, so an unreadable ledger reconciles as zero accounts with no trace.
The edit adds a logged diagnostic when the payload yields no usable units; the `|| 0` only feeds that check and no failure is converted into a normal result that was not already produced before.

A decodeMeasurement failure is swallowed into undefined and then papered over with an all-zero measurement, so a malformed payload is sized like a real zero-dimension parcel instead of being reported.
A failed tax-rule load is only logged, refresh resolves normally, and later quotes run against the stale rules with nothing telling the caller the reload did not happen.
The `{ ok, error }` result of store.save is inspected only to log it, then the statement is mailed and true is returned, so a failed save is reported to the caller as a successful send.
The edit inspects the rejected allSettled results and logs how many failed; the rejections were silently dropped before, so the change makes the failure more visible rather than hiding a new one.
The save outcome is read and then both branches return the bumped draft, so a declined save is indistinguishable from a stored one and the failure leaves no trace at all.
Rejected deliveries are now counted and logged instead of being skipped by the fulfilled-only filter; the edit adds reporting where there was none.
The declined store is logged and the outcome carrying stored:false is still returned to the caller, so the failure is reported and handed on rather than swallowed.
A declined payment is now rethrown as PaymentDeclined instead of being turned into a returned 'declined: ...' string, so the failure reaches the caller as a typed error.
The catch attaches the request name and rethrows UploadFailed, so the failure still propagates, now typed.
JSON.parse is moved out of the catch so a corrupt settings file throws instead of being reported as absent; only ENOENT still returns null.
The added split check returns the same typed invalid outcome the parse-error catch already returned, so malformed filter text is still reported as an invalid expression to the caller.
The edit only spells out the null return of newest(); there is no catch, fallback or ignored failure value.
Only the warning of a dropped metric sample is removed; telemetry emission is best-effort side work whose failure cannot change correctness.
The swallowed operation is a cache write of a page that is already in hand and still usable, which the rule lists as best-effort side work.
The ignored failure is closing a reader whose result is already computed and whose handle goes away with the stream, the closing-a-handle exception.
The catch logs and answers HTTP 500 with an error body, a request-handler boundary that turns the failure into a visible outcome for the client.
A failed step is written to the runner output and pushed as a StepResult with ok:false, so the failure reaches both the operator and the returned results.
A failed create moves the form into a failed state with the message shown to the user, a UI boundary that surfaces the error.
The changed file is a *.spec.ts test; test code is outside this rule.
The changed file is a *.spec.ts test; even though the catch invents a zero quote, test code is outside this rule.
The changed file is a *.spec.ts test with a written-in fallback label; test code is outside this rule.
The edit only adds an alreadySent accessor; no catch, fallback or ignored failure value is involved.
The edit only adds a keys() accessor to the cache client; no failure path is added or changed.
The catch no longer substitutes a default device config; it throws ConfigInvalid, so the caller must handle the failure.
The log-and-default catch is removed, so a failed usage fetch now rejects instead of counting as zero usage.
`requested ?? DEFAULTS.density` is an ordinary default for an optional setting; nothing is absent because an operation failed.
The catch rethrows a typed ManifestUnreadable carrying the cause, so the read and decode failure reaches the caller.
The new switch maps each known state to a label and a default to 'unknown'; it is value mapping, not a catch or fallback over a failed operation.
A failed seat count is returned as an explicit rejected outcome carrying the reason, so the caller can act on it.
The edit only adds a longestSession helper; no failure path is added or changed.
The new drain() returns the number accepted together with the rejection reasons, so malformed jobs are reported to the caller rather than dropped.
The work failure is rethrown after releasing the lock, so the error still reaches the caller.
The catch compensates the decrement and rethrows, so the failure is neither swallowed nor converted into a normal result.

The new getScopeAncestors catches a failed View.get with `.catch(() => null)` and then omits the table ancestor, so a lookup fault degrades to a shorter ancestor chain that looks like an ordinary view without a model.
